extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalism students, and practicing journalists interested in New Journalism / literary journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive guidance and evaluative criteria for producing or assessing New Journalism (literary/nonfiction narrative reporting) — its techniques, reporting practices, and common criticisms. Focuses on how to construct scenes, handle subjectivity, gather evidence, and preserve factual accuracy while using literary devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic literary techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: New Journalism is an artistic, creative, literary reporting form with dramatic literary techniques as one of its basic traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and advice in the article: use the imaginative resources of fiction (tension, symbol, cadence, irony, prosody, imagination), stream-of-consciousness and any literary device normally associated with novels and short stories. Wolfe and others argued writers may 'use any literary device' while still reporting factual events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensive reporting / saturation reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Saturation reporting: deep immersion in a subject, staying with it for days, weeks or longer to gather a depth of information not usually demanded in newspaper work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'locker room' or saturation approach underpins New Journalism: the writer delves deeply into a subject so they can report whole scenes and dialogues. Proponents argue it enhances accuracy; critics say immersion is inconsistent with objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of acknowledged subjectivity / subjective perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: New Journalism is characterized by a presence of subjective perspective and style; writers allow their opinion, ideas or involvement to creep into the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms include first-person 'I' voice, 'admitted' subjectivity, activist or advocacy stances, and participatory reporting. This posture is central to many definitions but is also a frequent target of criticism (e.g., accusations of rejecting objectivity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene-by-scene construction (scene as basic unit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic unit of reporting becomes the scene rather than isolated facts (who-what-when-where-how).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolfe emphasised 'telling the story using scenes'—scene construction underlies the 'sophisticated strategies of prose' used by New Journalists and enables narrative momentum akin to fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full record of dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Present dialogue in full—conversational speech rather than clipped quotations or paraphrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use full, lifelike dialogue to render scenes. This requires extensive reporting and often asking subjects directly about what was said/thought to reconstruct conversational detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-of-view (presenting scenes through a character's eyes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present every scene through the eyes of a particular character — use a clear point-of-view to shape narrative perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wolfe listed point-of-view as a main device borrowed from literary fiction; POV choice (first-person, third-person focalized, or the writer's own presence) affects tone and subjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording everyday incidental details / 'status life' indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Record minute, everyday details—behavior, possessions, friends and family—that reveal character and 'status life'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such incidental detail rounds out character sketches and supplies the novelistic texture New Journalists sought; intensive reporting is needed to capture trustworthy detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain strict factual accuracy (not fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite using fiction-like techniques, New Journalism 'is not fiction' and should maintain elements of reporting including 'strict adherence to factual accuracy' and the writer being the primary source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners state the work should be 'as reliable as the most reliable reportage' and seek 'larger truth' without inventing facts. Critics accuse some practitioners of 'juggling the facts' or fictionalizing details, so accuracy is a core evaluative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer as primary source / visible authorial voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer often functions as the primary source of the account and may be visibly present in the piece (the 'reporter himself' as part of the story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This visibility can enhance narrative immediacy (participatory reporting) but raises issues about subjectivity and the boundary between reporter and subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of interior monologue / methods to get 'inside the head' of subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques like interior monologue or reconstructing what subjects were thinking are used to represent mental life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers may ask subjects what they were thinking or feeling to justify representations of inner states; this method is controversial and must be grounded in rigorous reporting to avoid invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable literary devices and form (scene, dialogue, stream-of-consciousness, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: New Journalists claimed permission to use 'any literary device' from novels and short stories: scene construction, full dialogue, third-person POV, manifold incidental details, stream-of-consciousness and more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists Wolfe's four main devices and notes that the form 'mixes' novelistic devices with other prose techniques. Use of these devices is considered a defining technical characteristic when employed with rigorous reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid composite characters (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating composite characters—distilling a single named character from multiple real people—is a criticized practice that undermines credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Gail Sheehy 'Redpants' controversy is cited as an example where a composite character provoked outcry; journalists should avoid composites or be explicit about composites to preserve trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fictionalizing or 'juggling' facts to serve narrative (ethical limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictionalizing details or altering facts to achieve a 'larger reality' is a core criticism of New Journalism and an ethical boundary for reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics label such practices 'factual fiction' or 'parajournalism'; practitioners argue for larger truths but must resist inventing events or quotes. Accuracy and transparency are emphasized as defenses against this criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide verifiability / source transparency (respond to lack of footnotes criticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: The lack of source footnotes and bibliographies in many New Journalism works has been criticized as showing a lack of intellectual rigor and verifiability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To strengthen credibility, reporters should document reporting methods, sources, and be able to substantiate scenes and quotations even if conventional footnotes are not used in narrative magazines/books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of the objectivity vs. advocacy tension
rubrics_metrics.description: New Journalism often sits at the intersection of reportage and advocacy; writers must be aware that passionately subjective/activist reporting invites critique for abandoning objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some versions of New Journalism explicitly aim for advocacy or activism; others treat subjectivity as a tool for deeper truth. The writer should decide stance deliberately and address ethical implications.
